proposals.relationship: Challenges McPherson’s portrayal of the Freedmen Project as a self-emancipation orthodoxy that excludes Lincoln.
proposals.evidence_note: Own scanned essay29–33 calls this a caricature while acknowledging Lincoln’s centrality. Enslaved people are prime movers, not sole movers; citizens, soldiers, legislators and president retain distinct agency. Freedom, Free at Last and later volumes have collective editorial credit, including Barbara Jeanne Fields, Thavolia Glymph, Steven Miller, Joseph Reidy, Leslie Rowland and Julie Saville. Original McPherson paper and documentary volumes unread.
primary_locators: Printed29–33; collective credit note4 at29; final PDFpage8

proposals.relationship: As reported by Berlin, criticizes Berlin and the Freedmen Project for advancing a self-emancipation orthodoxy at Lincoln’s expense.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly Berlin’s attributed reconstruction of McPherson’s1992 AHA paper, printed28–29, not fresh reading of McPherson’s text. Robert Engs and Vincent Harding are co-targets; critique is not aimed at Berlin alone. Berlin contests the characterization and affirms complementary agency, a reply retained in the separate reverse edge. McPherson’s complete published versions unread.
primary_locators: Printed28–29; named targets and characterization at29

proposals.relationship: Uses Hofstadter’s bill-of-lading characterization as a rhetorical foil in discussing the Emancipation Proclamation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own scanned1996 essay30 reuses the attributed description;2001 Q&A qualifies its implication by emphasizing extraordinary effects despite flat wording. The speech calls it moral impact, whereas scanned essay says moral grandeur; do not silently merge as a verified original quotation. Original Hofstadter passage unread. This resource does not imply agreement that proclamation lacked political force.
primary_locators: 2001 Q&A answer to question beginning We know that the Emancipation Proclamation only legally

proposals.relationship: Identifies Davis’s slavery studies as guides to slavery’s double status as property and person and to abolition in the age of capitalism.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit authorial Prologue notes5–6 in displayed digital selection, with Hegel credited first in note5. Western Culture1966 and Age of Revolution1975 have distinct purposes. No direct first-edition collation or complete Prologue/book reading, and no general mentorship or causal debt inferred.

proposals.relationship: Identifies Roll, Jordan, Roll as the starting point for the contemporary debate on master-slave paternalism.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit evaluative authorial note6 in displayed digital notes; a resource for a debate, not assent to all of Genovese’s conclusions. Coexists with Berlin’s particular2003 chronological-scope criticism.1974 title/year are as cited by Berlin; the2001 speech reading list uses a different1976 edition. Both original editions and full Berlin Prologue unread.

proposals.relationship: Points to The Black Atlantic as a larger Atlantic perspective for understanding the formation of Black culture.
proposals.evidence_note: Own PartI note2 explicitly characterizes this resource; preceding co-credited Linebaugh/Rediker and Thornton works have different roles. Only selected authorial digital notes read, not the continuous chapter or original Gilroy book. No automatic founding or personal mentorship claim.

proposals.relationship: Questions the limited attention to slavery before1830 in Genovese’s nineteenth-century-centered historiography.
proposals.evidence_note: Only the fresh publisher opening extract of Berlin2003 article read. He groups Genovese with Kenneth Stampp, Stanley Elkins, John Blassingame, Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman and acknowledges their sharp disagreements. Do not infer rejection of paternalism, statistics or Marxism from this temporal-scope criticism; complete article and underlying books unread.

proposals.relationship: Defends the regional and chronological scope of Slaves Without Masters against Ely’s reported charge that Berlin equates restrictive law with daily life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2004 Foner review permits generalizations, regional comparisons and change over1790–1860 that a single-county study cannot provide, while valuing Ely’s local research. This is an explicitly bounded reception intervention; it neither certifies all Berlin findings nor credits Berlin with writing Foner’s reply. Original books unread.
primary_locators: Review paragraphs beginning Ely has done a remarkable job and Ely chides Berlin

proposals.relationship: Supplies Roediger with a formulation making African American family history central to the history of the working class.
proposals.evidence_note: Selected indexed own1993 paragraph128 expressly quotes Berlin’s1987 Gutman introduction46. Berlin mediates Gutman’s research agenda; note2 co-credits Montgomery/Gutman/Rawick interviews and retains Brody’s range-of-positions qualification. Not a claim Berlin founded Roediger’s full argument; complete article and Berlin’s original introduction unread.
primary_locators: Printed128 paragraph beginning The tardiness of U.S. labor historians; note2

proposals.relationship: Uses Curtin’s discussion of the expanding meanings of creole before specifying his own Atlantic-creole terminology.
proposals.evidence_note: Own selected digital PartI note1 explicitly quotes and attributes Curtin Economic Change in Precolonial Africa1975 pp138–139n5, then warns that creole has no universally accepted usage and states his own definitions. This is bounded conceptual use from an authorial note, not a general genealogy or direct reading of Curtin’s complete book; cited original and continuous Berlin chapter unread.
